issues.title: [Bug][ROCm] GLM-5.3-Flash fails to boot on 0.3.1 nightly: SparseAttnIndexerKpool (AMD) missing forward_cuda → NotImplementedError
issues.body:
## [Bug][ROCm] GLM-5.3-Flash fails to boot on v0.29.1rc0 nightly: SparseAttnIndexerKpool (AMD) missing forward_cuda → NotImplementedError

### Current behavior

Serving GLM-5.3-Flash on the latest ROCm nightly (`vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-0bfc7a15d`, `vv0.29.1rc0.dev265+g0bfc7a15d`) crashes at `profile_run` on every worker rank:

```
(APIServer ... ) RuntimeError: Worker failed with error ''ROCMAiterMLASparseImpl' object has no attribute 'record_logical_topk_ready''
```

*(that one is #57248 / #57252 / #56604 — patched separately)*

and, with that patched, the next blocker is:

```
File "vllm/model_executor/custom_op.py", line 149, in forward_hip
    return self.forward_cuda(*args, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
File "vllm/model_executor/custom_op.py", line 145, in forward_cuda
    raise NotImplementedError
NotImplementedError
```

raised from `SparseAttnIndexerKpool` (`vllm/models/glm5next/common/attention.py:392` → `self.indexer_op(...)`).

### Root cause

`CustomOp.dispatch_forward` routes **enabled** ops to `forward_hip` on ROCm, and `forward_hip` falls back to `forward_cuda`. The AMD implementation of `SparseAttnIndexerKpool` (`vllm/models/glm5next/amd/sparse_indexer.py`, registered as `sparse_attn_indexer_kpool`) defines **only `forward_native`** — no `forward_cuda` — so any run where the op is enabled raises `NotImplementedError` at the first forward.

On this nightly the resolved `compilation_config.custom_ops` contains `'all'` (seen in the engine init log), which enables every registered op and triggers this deterministically.

The NVIDIA implementation (`nvidia/sparse_indexer.py`) defines both `forward_native` and `forward_cuda`; the AMD one is missing the alias the ROCm dispatch requires.

### Proposed fix

Alias at class level:

```python
SparseAttnIndexerKpool.forward_cuda = SparseAttnIndexerKpool.forward_native
```

(or define `forward_cuda` as a method calling `forward_native`), mirroring the NVIDIA implementation.

### Environment

- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-0bfc7a15d095fe83ecc82b50561a93c177fece2d` (`vv0.29.1rc0.dev265+g0bfc7a15d`)
- Hardware: 8× AMD MI350X (gfx950), TP8
- Model: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` (fp8), `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-model-len 524288`
- aiter `2693202`

### Verification

With the one-line alias applied in-place, the engine boots Ready (57 FULL + 106 PIECEWISE cudagraphs) and passes a chunked-prefill repro plus a long-context ladder up to 524,212 tokens with zero memory access faults.

Related threads: #57227 (original MAF, root-caused by #57317), #57248 (nightly boot regressions), #57252, #56604, #57192.

issues.title: [Feature]: Production evidence for restoring concurrent partial prefill limits (max_num_partial_prefills / max_concurrent_prefills) in V1 scheduler
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Motivation

We operate a production vLLM deployment (GLM-based MoE model, TP=4, 4x NVIDIA B200,
V1 engine) serving a workload dominated by very long prompts (RAG/long-context,
median ~100k-180k prompt tokens per request, generation typically <1k tokens).
Under this workload we consistently observe severe TTFT tail latency caused by
head-of-line blocking in prefill scheduling, and we believe this is a strong
real-world case for reviving #49075 / #55256.

## Problem

With `--enable-chunked-prefill` and `--max-num-batched-tokens` set to a
reasonably high value (tested 8192 and 16384), a single long-prompt request
still needs many scheduler iterations to complete its prefill
(prompt_tokens / max_num_batched_tokens ≈ 7-12 iterations for our 100k-180k
token prompts). Because the V1 scheduler currently has **no cap on concurrent
partial prefills**, any request queued behind one of these long prefills must
wait for it to fully finish before its own prefill can start — there is no
way to interleave multiple partial prefills to give newer/shorter requests a
fair share of the per-step token budget.

We attempted to mitigate this with `--max-num-partial-prefills 4` (docs suggest
this exists as a `SchedulerConfig` field), which immediately fails:

vllm: error: unrecognized arguments: --max-num-partial-prefills 4

Digging into this, we found the flag was intentionally removed from
`vllm/config/scheduler.py` in #49244 (V0 cleanup, July 2026) as "dead config"
because it had no V1 consumer, and issue #39737 confirms the same failure mode
on an earlier vLLM version (`NotImplementedError: Concurrent Partial Prefill
is not supported`) with no maintainer response since April 2026. #49075
attempts to restore and properly enforce these fields in the V1 scheduler but
is currently open, unrebased, has an unresolved CodeRabbit finding on the
WAITING-loop admission check, and has never had CI run. #55256 proposed a
simpler, threshold-independent `max_concurrent_prefills` knob with a
supporting benchmark, but was closed by the author without maintainer
feedback.

## Production evidence

During a saturation window on our GLM deployment, we captured the following
via `vllm:*` Prometheus histograms (median values from `histogram_quantile`
over live traffic, not synthetic benchmarks):

| Metric | Healthy baseline | Saturated window |
|---|---|---|
| TTFT p50 | ~0.5-0.9 s | up to **18 s** |
| TTFT p95 | ~2-4 s | up to **76 s** |
| Request queue time p50 | ~0.2 s | up to **12 s** |
| Inter-token latency p50 | ~20-40 ms | up to **247 ms** |
| `num_requests_waiting{reason="capacity"}` | 0 | 0-9, sustained |
| `num_requests_running` | 20-30 | 17-28 (unchanged — not a concurrency-limit issue) |
| `kv_cache_usage_perc` | <40% | <40% (unchanged — **not KV pressure**) |
| GPU util (DCGM) | 90-99% | 96-99% (unchanged) |
| GPU tensor-pipe active (DCGM) | n/a | **only 10-20%** |
| `num_preemptions_total` increase | 0 | 0 |

The combination of high GPU utilization with low tensor-core activity, zero
KV cache pressure, zero preemptions, and a queue whose only wait reason is
`capacity` strongly indicates the bottleneck is *prefill scheduling
admission*, not compute, memory, or the `max_num_seqs` concurrency cap. Even
after doubling `--max-num-batched-tokens` from 8192 to 16384, the p50 stayed
healthy (~0.5-1s) but p90/p95/p99 remained disproportionately high
(9.6s / 14.5s / 18.9s during a moderate-traffic window) — consistent with a
minori

issues.title: [RFC]: Layer-Wise Mixed-Precision KV Cache
issues.body:
Status: Draft for discussion. Scope: the three-part vLLM implementation stack plus a proposed manager-block optimization follow-up. Cache calculations below evaluate this full stacked design; the optimization is not enabled by the three current PRs.

## Summary

Allow a model to use different KV-cache formats in different attention layers, initially full FP8 K/V and full NVFP4 K/V. Preserve each layer's logical encoding through dispatch and allocation, and support both attention-only models and hybrid attention/Mamba models using existing attention kernels and the heterogeneous cache-packing infrastructure already used by DeepSeek V4.

This is **layer-wise** mixed precision. FP8 K with NVFP4 V inside the same layer is a separate feature and is not enabled by this RFC.

## Motivation

Layers can have different sensitivity to KV quantization. A checkpoint should be able to retain FP8 in selected layers and use NVFP4 elsewhere, without requiring a model-wide format or changes to attention kernels.

Two runtime assumptions make this difficult:

- Physical tensor dtype alone does not fully describe the KV encoding or scales.
- Legacy hybrid allocation couples attention block sizing to recurrent-state page sizes. Adding attention formats with different byte sizes can increase alignment requirements, padding, and prefix-cache block granularity.

The proposal separates logical encoding from physical page allocation. It enables quality/memory trade-off experiments; it does not prescribe the optimal layer recipe or claim an accuracy improvement for every model.

## Proposed Change

```text
ModelOpt checkpoint recipe       Explicit global KV dtype override
             |                                  |
             +----------> Effective per-layer dtype
                                      |
                          AttentionSpec.cache_dtype
                              /                 \
                 Backend dtype dispatch     Exact cache-page specs
                          |                         |
                 Existing FP8/NVFP4 kernels  Packed block-pool allocation
```

### 1. Preserve Logical Dtype

Add `AttentionSpec.cache_dtype` and the generic `QuantizationConfig.get_kv_cache_dtype(prefix)` hook, defaulting to `None`. Preserve logical dtype and quantization mode during spec merges, and reject conflicting formats.

FlashInfer uses an explicit global KV dtype first, then a concrete per-spec dtype. An ambiguous quantized spec fails clearly instead of guessing its encoding. Existing unquantized behavior and skip-layer precedence are retained.

### 2. Reuse DeepSeek V4 Cache Packing

DeepSeek V4 already needs caches with different page sizes, such as MLA, indexer, and sliding-window caches. vLLM's existing infrastructure represents those pages separately and packs compatible layers into cache groups. We reuse that mechanism for pages whose sizes differ because of FP8/NVFP4 encoding.

| Existing mechanism | Reuse for layer-wise mixed precision |
|---|---|
| `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` | Retain each layer's exact spec and page size within a compatible group. |
| `_get_packed_kv_cache_groups()` | Group layers by compatible cache behavior, without requiring identical page sizes. |
| Block-outer allocation and per-layer offsets/strides | Place FP8 and NVFP4 pages side by side and expose each layer's view to its existing kernel. |
| Shared block pool | Size rows for the widest packed group; a block ID belongs to one group at a time. |

`enable_adaptive_verification` is left **false** because adaptive DSpark is currently broken on SM90 ([#54011](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54011)).

issues.title: [Bug]: AriaForConditionalGeneration.load_weights discards loaded parameter set, making weight tracking ineffective
issues.body:
## Description

On current `main`, `AriaForConditionalGeneration.load_weights()` invokes `AutoWeightsLoader.load_weights()` but discards the returned loaded-parameter set:

```python
def load_weights(self, weights: Iterable[tuple[str, torch.Tensor]]):
    loader = AutoWeightsLoader(self)
    loader.load_weights(weights, mapper=self.hf_to_vllm_mapper)
```

This changes loader behavior beyond the missing return annotation.

`DefaultModelLoader.load_weights()` uses the model's return value as the input to weight tracking:

```python
loaded_weights = model.load_weights(...)

default_enable_weights_track = (
    model_config.quantization is None and loaded_weights is not None
)

enable_weights_track = (
    self.enable_weights_track
    if self.enable_weights_track is not None
    else default_enable_weights_track
)

if enable_weights_track:
    self.track_weights_loading(model, loaded_weights)
```

`track_weights_loading()` then performs its missing-parameter comparison only when `loaded_weights is not None`:

```python
weights_to_load = {name for name, _ in model.named_parameters()}

if loaded_weights is not None:
    ...
    weights_not_loaded = weights_to_load - loaded_weights
    if weights_not_loaded:
        raise ValueError(...)
```

As a result, Aria has two related behaviors:

```text
Default configuration:
    load_weights() -> None
    -> default_enable_weights_track=False
    -> missing-weight validation is skipped

enable_weights_track=True:
    load_weights() -> None
    -> track_weights_loading(model, None)
    -> comparison is still skipped
```

So explicitly enabling `enable_weights_track` does not restore the validation for Aria.

This matters because Aria contains checkpoint-populated parameters allocated with `torch.empty`, including the projector query parameter and MoE router weights. An incomplete checkpoint should therefore be caught by the same initialized-from-checkpoint validation used by other models rather than silently bypassing that validation layer.

## Expected behavior

Propagate the set returned by `AutoWeightsLoader`:

```python
def load_weights(
    self,
    weights: Iterable[tuple[str, torch.Tensor]],
) -> set[str]:
    loader = AutoWeightsLoader(self)
    return loader.load_weights(weights, mapper=self.hf_to_vllm_mapper)
```

This allows `DefaultModelLoader` to perform its normal missing-weight check.

## Suggested regression test

A regression test does not need to run inference. It can exercise an Aria weight load with a deliberately incomplete weight iterator and verify that non-quantized loading reports the omitted parameter.

It would also be useful to verify the explicit:

```text
model_loader_extra_config={"enable_weights_track": True}
```

case so this configuration cannot silently become ineffective again.

## Provenance

Verified against vLLM `main` at:

```text
ac78445bc9ee3bb615b8b21db22fb7dac6698ece
```

Relevant files:

```text
vllm/model_executor/models/aria.py
vllm/model_executor/model_loader/default_loader.py
```

issues.title: [Bug][ROCm] GLM-5.3-Flash kpool indexer overwrites its own KV cache: backend advertises a kernel block size the kernels do not use
issues.body:
### Summary

On ROCm, the GLM-5.3-Flash kpool sparse indexer **silently overwrites its own KV cache**. 4096 pool entries are written into 864 distinct slots, so ~79 % of the indexer's keys are wrong. The model still produces fluent text, so nothing crashes — long-context recall just degrades, and `temperature=0` stops being reproducible because the damage depends on which physical blocks the allocator hands out.

This is **ROCm-only** and distinct from #40018 (whose fix, #43781, is present in the tree I tested).

### Root cause

`DeepseekV32IndexerBackend.get_supported_kernel_block_sizes()` (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py`):

```python
return [1, MultipleOf(16)] if current_platform.is_rocm() else [64]
```

On CUDA the backend declares exactly `[64]`, so vLLM sets `kernel_block_size = 64`, `BlockTable.use_hybrid_blocks = True`, and builds a kernel-granular block table. On ROCm it declares "any multiple of 16", so the hybrid aligner's choice (640 tokens here) is taken as natively supported: `blocks_per_kv_block == 1`, **no kernel-granular block table**.

But the kernels do not read 640-token blocks. DeepGEMM/AITER paged-MQA reads pool pages of 32 states; with `tokens_per_state == index_kpool == 4` that is 128 tokens. So the storage block (640 tok = 160 states) is five pages, and both `slot_mapping` and `cp_gather_indexer_k_quant_cache_triton` address it with the **page** size (32) while the block table holds **spec-block** ids — a 5x over-subscription.

The intended split is even documented in `vllm/models/glm5next/nvidia/attention.py` as `storage_kernel_block_size`, but that identifier appears nowhere else in the tree — it was never implemented.

### Evidence (8x MI350X, gfx950, TP8, ROCm 7.2.3, `index_kpool=4`, `block_size=640`)

Instrumented at the indexer, two identical requests, prefix caching off:

| | before | after fix |
|---|---|---|
| distinct cache slots written (of 4096 pools) | **864** | **4096** |
| `max_slot` | 863 (= 26x32+31) | 4159 (= 26x160+…) |
| distinct gathered K rows (of 4000) | **864** | **4000** |
| rows duplicated at period 256 | 3488 | **0** |
| block-table entries used | 27/125, **99 zeros** | 125/125, 0 zeros |
| block-table width | 205 | 1025 (= 205x5) |

Zero entries are not skipped: the gather clamps an invalid block to `safe_block_id = 0` and reads physical block 0 repeatedly.

Layer-by-layer hashing of two identical requests shows the divergence starting exactly at layer 3, the first `deepseek_sparse_attention` layer, while `q`, `gate_score`, `ape` and the pre-pool `k` are bit-identical — only the gathered `k_quant` differs.

### Reproducer

Needle-in-a-haystack, needle at 50 %, `temperature=0`, ~40k tokens:

```
before:  3/3 missed   (model never finds the key)
after:   3/3 found
```

Sweep on the fixed build (tuned config, compiled, prefix caching on):

| prompt tokens | needle |
|---|---|
| 6 687 | found |
| 27 141 | found |
| 54 265 | found |
| 110 561 | found |

### Fix

Let the indexer cache advertise the kernel block size its kernels actually use, so vLLM's existing `use_hybrid_blocks` machinery builds the kernel-granular block table:

```python
# vllm/models/glm5next/nvidia/attention.py
class Glm5NextIndexerCache(DeepseekV32IndexerCache):
    def get_attn_backend(self):
        # DeepGEMM paged-MQA reads pool pages of 32 or 64 states; with
        # tokens_per_state == index_kpool that is 32*kpool / 64*kpool tokens.
        return _kpool_indexer_backend(self._index_kpool)   # -> [32*k

issues.title: [Bug][ROCm] Engine stops making progress inside an aiter fused MoE step on gfx942, then dies with no error (GLM-5.3, TP8, v0.29.0)
issues.body:
## Problem

On 8x MI325X (gfx942), the engine stops making progress under normal load. Generation falls from over 2,000 tokens a second to zero between two log samples that are ten seconds apart. The same requests stay resident and the KV cache stays at about a fifth full, so this is not an out of memory condition and nothing is preempted.

Some freezes clear after a few seconds. Some never clear. When a freeze does not clear, the engine dies and no worker writes an error. There is no traceback, no HIP error, no memory access fault and no watchdog message.

| Reading | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Fatal engine deaths | 4 in 6 days |
| Freezes that cleared | at least 6, from 75 s to 12.8 min |
| Short pauses in one 5.4 hour soak | 29, about 10 s each |
| Serve blocks affected | 3 or more |
| Same test on gfx950 (MI355X) | 16,026 requests, zero errors, zero pauses |

## Environment

- vLLM `v0.29.0`, image `docker.io/vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.29.0`. A derived image that adds only the `fastokens` package behaves the same.
- 8x AMD Instinct MI325X, gfx942, 256 GB HBM each. Single node, Kubernetes. ROCm 7.2.3.
- Model `zai-org/GLM-5.3`, block-scaled FP8, `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`, served from local weights.
- `--tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 262144`, MTP speculative decode with 5 tokens.
- `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`, `VLLM_EXECUTE_MODEL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1800`, `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`, `NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS=112`.

## What the logs show

Two consecutive engine samples, ten seconds apart:

```
INFO 09-15 22:57:25 [loggers.py:310] Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 851.4 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 1095.8 tokens/s, Running: 56 reqs, Waiting: 6 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 21.9%
INFO 09-15 22:57:35 [loggers.py:310] Engine 000: Avg prompt throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Running: 56 reqs, Waiting: 6 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 21.9%
```

Just before that sample, all eight workers log the same aiter fused MoE dispatch for a batch width that is new to the run:

```
[aiter] [fused_moe] using 1stage (kernelName1='_ZN5aiter46fmoe_bf16_blockscaleFp8_g1u1_vs_ps_silu_64x256E', kernelName2=nan) for ('gfx942', 304, 2048, 6144, 256, 257, 9, 'ActivationType.Silu', 'torch.bfloat16', 'torch.float8_e4m3fnuz', 'torch.float8_e4m3fnuz', 'QuantType.per_1x128', True, False)
```

After that the EngineCore writes one line a minute and nothing else:

```
INFO [shm_broadcast.py:801] No available shared memory broadcast block found in 60 seconds.
```

During the freeze, `rocm-smi` inside the pod reads two GPUs at 100 percent use and six at 0 percent. VRAM is flat at 90 percent on all eight, which is the memory reserved at startup.

When a freeze is fatal, the sequence is the same and it does not recover. The engine is silent for 12 minutes and 23 seconds, then the EngineCore raises `RuntimeError: cancelled` from `shm_broadcast.acquire_read` and the API server raises `EngineDeadError`. The only line any worker writes in that window is `Parent process exited, terminating worker queues`.

## How to reproduce on an MI325X box

We cannot give a small script, because the freeze needs many requests in flight. These are the conditions that produce it, and it has fired on every block we have run for more than 20 minutes at this concurrency.

1. Serve GLM 5.3 FP8 at tensor parallel 8 with the flags above, including MTP with 5 speculative tokens.
2. Send between 50 and 60 concurrent chat requests. Use long prompts, about 50,000 tokens, with shared prefixes

### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Your current environment

- vLLM **0.25.1** (pip wheel), 1× **H100 80GB (SM90)**, torch 2.9.0, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.12
- The affected kernel source (`csrc/libtorch_stable/moe/marlin_moe_wna16/marlin_template.h`) is **byte-identical between v0.25.1 and current `main`**, so this should still reproduce on main.
- Model: `openai/gpt-oss-20b` requantized to ModelOpt-style **NVFP4 W4A16** (`quant_algo: NVFP4`, group 16), served on Hopper via the Marlin FP4 MoE fallback (`fused_marlin_moe` → `ops.moe_wna16_marlin_gemm`). MoE dims: E=32 experts, top_k=4, hidden=2880, intermediate=2880.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**When `mul_topk_weights=True`, `moe_wna16_marlin_gemm` applies the WRONG per-row routing weight at these shapes** — each output row is multiplied by *a different row's* `topk_weights` entry, by 0.0, or (in-engine) by garbage read from shared memory. End-to-end this makes gpt-oss-20b NVFP4 on Hopper generate garbage (huge/NaN logits → repeated token; we observed intermediate values ~1e33 = output × a garbage bf16 multiplier).

The same call with `mul_topk_weights=False` (and the multiply applied externally on the output rows) is correct to kernel noise — with bit-identical weights, activations, and scheduling metadata.

#### Isolation trail (standalone replay of a captured failing `fused_marlin_moe` call, exact fp32 reference)

| variant | result |
|---|---|
| gemm1 (w13), as captured | all rows match (maxrel ≤ 3e-3) |
| gemm2 (w2), as captured (`top_k=1, mul_topk_weights=True` — the config `fused_marlin_moe` uses when `apply_router_weight_on_input=False`) | **128/128 rows corrupt, out_absmax ≈ 4e+32** |
| gemm2, same args, `mul_topk_weights=False` + external multiply | all rows match (maxrel 2.4e-3) |
| sweeps: thread configs, `use_atomic_add`, `use_fp32_reduce`, moe_block_size | failure unaffected |
| random weight values instead of real checkpoint | still fails → value-independent |
| small shapes (e.g. E=8, N=K=512) | pass → layout/shape-dependent |

#### Forensic: the wrong multiplier is another row's topk weight

In the minimal repro below, dividing each corrupted output row by its (bias-free) unweighted reference reveals the factor that was actually applied. It is **another row's routing weight, bf16-exact, or 0.0**:

issues.title: [RFC][ROCm]: Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) for DeepSeek-V4 hybrid SWA + compressed KV cache
issues.body:
### Motivation.

## Motivation

DeepSeek-V4 is MLA-based (1 latent KV head), so under TP, every rank stores a full replica of the KV cache. This means TP8 spends ~8x the KV memory than technically required, leading to reduced HBM headroom. DCP removes this replication by sharding the KV cache along the sequence dimension. On agentic workloads with huge sequence lengths (comprising mostly of prefill work) and heavy cache pressure, aggregate KV capacity is the dominant lever for being able to fit many requests in the cache and achieve high throughput. DP-attention also solves this problem, but can suffer from very high latency, especially when a single GPU is computing a large uncached prefill.






### Proposed Change.

## Scope / Hardware

Primary target is **ROCm on MI355X (gfx950)**. All development and validation runs on an 8xMI355X node. The ROCm/AITER leg is the focus of this work. Most of the work is vendor-neutral in nature (scheduler geometry, ownership/layout math, compressor Triton kernels, merge collectives, etc.), but we focus on MI355X for validation and performance optimization. The NVIDIA/FlashMLA attention leg is transplanted from #44573 directly, however we have no NVIDIA hardware to validate it.


## Current State

#44573 (DCP) and #43809 (PCP) by @baonudesifeizhai implemented DSV4 CP for the NVIDIA/FlashMLA path in May/June, however both are inactive since June and predate the mainline DCP framework consolidation. The merged K3 DCP stack from #51705 (decode-LSE) and #53598 (per-group cache geometry) provides the framework upon which this line of PRs is being built. However, no DSV4 model-specific support in vllm/models/deepseek_v4/ currently has the necessary DCP wiring. Additionally, mainline's DCP support currently does not support deduplication for DSV4's SWA/compressed groups.


## Proposal

We are implementing DSV4 DCP as a new PR series on top of the current main and with ongoing efforts to support DCP on other models such as Kimi-K3. Current draft PRs are here (WIP draft: <TODO>), and focuses on transplanting the validated #44573 mechanisms to the currently merged framework. The overall structure of the ongoing contribution is detailed below:

1) Interleaved position ownership with logical block tables, so prefix caching works on sharded DSV4 groups. Needs design alignment with the #53598 geometry (see below).
2) Compressor under DCP: per-rank partial softmax-pool stats -> 1 all-gather/all-reduce merge -> owner-masked cache insert.
3) Sink-free local attention returns LSE, cross-rank merge via mainline collectives such as dcp_a2a_lse_reduce / cp_lse_ag_out_rs, attn sink applied only once after merge has completed.
4) ROCm leg: LSE return + deferred sink for DSV4 sparse split-K/ragged Triton kernels, Triton topk twin for CuteDSL-only indexer merge, DCP wiring for DeepSeekV4ROCMAiterMLAAttention.forward_mqa. Validation on 8xMI355X (gfx950).
5) interleave=1 only initially, to adhere to the sparse-indexer gate. Future work could involve allowing other interleaving degrees if there is potential performance benefit.


## Asks

1) **Cache Geometry**: we are extending dcp_world_size_for_kv_cache_spec to respect the supports_context_parallel flag. Is the current design compatible with the AMD roadmap for hybrid cache DCP? cc @tjtanaa @YukioZzz @okorzh-amd 
2) **AITER**: the gfx950 OPUS sparse prefill (pa_sparse_prefill_opus) returns output only without LSE. For the initial implementation, DCP>1 prefill falls back to th

issues.title: [Bug]: Weight-loading/repacking memory is not reclaimed on discrete GPUs, forcing lower max-num-seqs / max-num-batched-tokens (Kimi K3, B200, fastsafetensors + DeepEP v2)
issues.body:
### Your current environment



- vLLM `v0.28.0`, `vllm/vllm-openai` container image
- 2–4 nodes x 8x NVIDIA **B200 SXM** (discrete GPU, 180 GB), GKE + LeaderWorkerSet
- Model: `moonshotai/Kimi-K3` (`mxfp4`), `--load-format fastsafetensors`, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`
- Parallelism: TP4/TP8 + DP + `--enable-expert-parallel` (EP16 / EP32)
- All-to-all backends tested: **DeepEP v2** and NCCL (gIB RoCE)
- `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1`
- Also reproduced with speculative decoding (draft model `Inferact/Kimi-K3-DSpark`)



### 🐛 Describe the bug


On discrete GPUs, memory used during weight loading and `process_weights_after_loading` is retained inside PyTorch's caching allocator pool (`reserved - allocated`) rather than returned to the CUDA driver before the engine initializes communication buffers, profiles KV cache, or loads secondary models. In practice this causes startup OOM or forces significantly lower batch capacity.

**Observed behavior (reproducible):**

1. **2-node DeepEP v2 (`TP8_DP2_EP16`)** — with `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.88`, `--max-num-seqs 256 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192` OOMs during startup. Without a patch, we have to clamp parameters down to `--max-num-seqs 32 --max-num-batched-tokens 512 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.80`, which severely limits throughput.
2. **Speculative decoding (target `Kimi-K3` + draft `Kimi-K3-DSpark`, both via `fastsafetensors`)** — exhibits the same startup memory exhaustion pressure.
3. **With a 4-line memory cleanup patch injected into `process_weights_after_loading`, both workloads start cleanly and allow raising `--max-num-seqs` / `--max-num-batched-tokens` back up to `256 / 8192`:**

```python
def process_weights_after_loading(
    model: nn.Module, model_config: ModelConfig, target_device: torch.device
) -> None:
    import gc
    gc.collect()
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    ...
```

### Empirical VRAM Measurements (2x 8×B200 nodes, `TP8_DP2_EP16`, `v0.28.0`)

We instrumented `BaseModelLoader.load_model()` (`vllm/model_executor/model_loader/base_loader.py`) on 2x 8×B200 hosts (`178.351 GiB` total HBM per GPU) running `moonshotai/Kimi-K3` (`mxfp4`) + `Inferact/Kimi-K3-DSpark` with `--load-format fastsafetensors`:

| Model / Boundary | Arm A: Unpatched (`reserved_GiB` / `resv - alloc`) | Arm A: **`driver_free_GiB`** (`cudaMemGetInfo`) | Arm B: With `gc.collect() + empty_cache()` (`EMPTYCACHE_RETURNED`) | Arm B: **`driver_free_GiB`** (`cudaMemGetInfo`) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **`Kimi-K3`: `05_before_load_weights`** | `129.352 GiB` (`0.286 GiB`) | `46.338 GiB` | `129.352 GiB` (`0.000 GiB`) | `46.338 GiB` |

issues.title: [Bug]: Wrong timestamps if audio > 30s
issues.body:
### Your current environment


NA

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Segment level timestamps are incrementally offset by ~0.5s per segment.**

When transcribing long audio with vLLM Whisper, segment-level timestamps are increasingly inaccurate. Chunking uses by default a 1s window to find low-energy (quiet) regions for splitting, so the next chunk may start up to 1s earlier than the nominal chunk length. This offset is not compensated for when generating segment timestamps, resulting in an average delay of ~0.5s per segment, which accumulates (e.g., 5s after 10 segments).

Clients can workaround by subtracting 0.5s per segment, but that's obviously not accurate.

Also, the [related documentation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/e83b7e379c11bf136c1b96bc6a67b6d2207cfde4/docs/contributing/model/transcription.md#audio-preprocessing-and-chunking) is not correct: there are no overlapping chunks, but just a window for searching the best split point. Maybe this confusion is the cause of the issue.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

issues.title: [Performance]: Streaming derender bypasses renderer thread pool and blocks the event loop
issues.body:
### Your current environment

- vllm version: v0.28.0
- Architecture: AArch64
- Deployment: vLLM Render as a sidecar
- Request type: streaming Chat Completions
- Concurrent requests: 20
- Output length: up to 2048 tokens
- `--renderer-num-workers`: tested with both `4` and `8`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Streaming Derender appears to perform CPU-bound detokenization directly on the FastAPI event loop instead of using the renderer thread pool.

Under concurrent streaming workloads, this serializes Derender processing, increases per-chunk latency, delays tokenization requests, and propagates backpressure to the inference engine.

This looks related to, but not fully covered by, [#49396](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49396), which offloaded existing Derender CPU work to the renderer thread pool.

## Observed implementation

The non-streaming Derender paths use asynchronous wrappers backed by the renderer executor.

However, the streaming paths call synchronous detokenization directly from async code:

- `OnlineDerenderer.derender_chat_stream()`
- `OnlineDerenderer.derender_completion_stream()`
- `_detokenize_delta()`

As a result, increasing `--renderer-num-workers` does not improve streaming Derender throughput.

## Benchmark results

| Metric | 4 workers | 8 workers |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Aggregate throughput | 889.1 tok/s | 899.5 tok/s |
| Per-stream throughput p50 | 46.3 tok/s | 46.0 tok/s |
| Derender RPC latency p50 | 21.35 ms | 21.52 ms |
| Chunk cadence p50 | 21.49 ms | 21.66 ms |
| Tokenize latency p50 | 153.8 ms | 155.4 ms |

Compared with the Render-disabled baseline:

| Metric | Render disabled | Streaming Render |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Aggregate throughput | 1011.6 tok/s | 889.1 tok/s |
| Per-stream throughput p50 | 53.1 tok/s | 46.3 tok/s |
| TTFT p50 | 166 ms | 167 ms |
| TTOT p50 | 18.70 ms | 21.26 ms |

The workload completed successfully without request errors.

## Additional timing evidence

For the streaming Derender consumer:

| Measurement | p50 |
| --- | ---: |
| Derender RPC time | 21.35 ms |
| RPC plus local processing | 21.40 ms |
| Chunk consumption cadence | 21.49 ms |
| Queue wait time | 0.15 ms |

The timing approximately satisfies:

```text
chunk cadence
~= queue wait + Derender processing
~= Derender RPC latency
```

This indicates that the streaming consumption loop is paced almost entirely by the synchronous Derender request.

The same RPC takes approximately 3.2 ms under light load but approximately 21.4 ms at concurrency 20, indicating event-loop saturation and queuing.

## Additional context: token-only Generate does not provide batch streaming

The token-only `/inference/v1/generate` endpoint currently handles one prompt or sequence per request. Therefore, a multi-prompt Completion request must be fanned out into multiple independent Generate streams.

Each generated stream maintains its own Derender `stream_state` and invokes the streaming Derender endpoint for every chunk:

```text
multi-prompt request
  -> N Generate streams
  -> N independent Derender states
  -> one Derender request per generated chunk
```

This is not the direct cause of the event-loop blocking issue, which is also reproducible with concurrent single-prompt requests. However, the lack of a batch Generate interface amplifies the problem because the number of concurrent per-chunk Derender calls grows with the number of generated sequences.

It may be useful to clarify whether batch token-only Generate is planned. Rega

issues.title: [Bug][ROCm][Attention][KV Connector] DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5.x DSA sparse-MLA decode is garbage under CUDA graphs in PD-disaggregation (remote-prefilled KV)
issues.body:
## Summary
In PD-disaggregated serving on ROCm/MI300X (MoRIIO KV connector, WideEP DP8/EP8), the **decode** engine emits degenerate repeated-token garbage (`locklocklock…` / `!!!`) for **remote-prefilled** requests whenever decode runs under **any CUDA-graph capture** (`FULL`, `PIECEWISE`, or `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`). With `DECODE_CUDAGRAPH_MODE=NONE` (eager) the identical stack decodes **coherently**. Colocated (non-disagg) serving and vLLM v0.27.1 are unaffected.

## Environment
- vLLM **0.28.0** (`vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.28.0`), AITER 0.1.19, ROCm 7.2.3
- 2× **MI300X (gfx942)**, RoCEv2; KV connector = **MoRIIOConnector** (WRITE mode), `block_size=1`, fp8 KV
- Models: **GLM-5.3-FP8** and **GLM-5.1-FP8** (both `GlmMoeDsa`, DeepSeek-V3.2-style **DSA sparse-MLA**)
- Topology: 1P1D **WideEP DP8/EP8**; MTP on or off (does not matter)

## How to reproduce
1. Launch 1P1D PD-disagg (MoRIIO WRITE) — e.g. the AMD harness `.buildkite/amd-disagg/run-slurm-disagg-test.sh` with `WIDE_EP_MODE=1 MORIIO_READ_MODE=0` — using `DECODE_CUDAGRAPH_MODE=FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`.
2. Send any request → decode returns `locklocklock…` (garbage).
3. Set `DECODE_CUDAGRAPH_MODE=NONE` (eager) → decode is coherent. (`FULL` and `PIECEWISE` are each garbage too.)

## Expected behavior
Decode under CUDA graphs produces the same coherent output as eager decode (and as colocated single-node / vLLM v0.27.1).

## Isolation — what did NOT fix it vs what WORKED
We walked the full transfer→decode path with per-step, on-device instrumentation applied identically to both engines.

**Did NOT fix it (still garbage), i.e. ruled out as the cause:**
- **KV-cache content / transfer** — the transfer is complete and **bit-exact** (producer == consumer bytes for every layer, including the sparse-indexer k_cache). Explicitly transferring the indexer k_cache changed nothing.
- **MoRI library version** — swapping v1.1.0 ↔ commit `42e895472b08` (the version used by the working v0.27.1 recipe) made no difference.
- **MoRI-EP `combine()` fix** (#56073 / ROCm/mori#475) — inert here (our EP8 runs the single-node **IntraNode** combine, not the InterNodeV1 path that fix targets).
- **Decode metadata** — byte-identical local-vs-remote for the same prompt (`num_computed_tokens`, positions, seq_len, block_table, indexer top-k, and post-remap global KV slots all match). Nothing to correct.
- **KV dtype** — reproduces with **fp8 and bf16** (so not an fp8-scale/dequant issue).
- **Transfer mode** — reproduces in **both READ and WRITE** MoRIIO modes.
- **MTP** — reproduces with speculative decode **on and off**.
- **Widening the eager CUDA-graph region** — restoring a broad `eager_break_during_capture` over the whole sparse decode (breakable/PIECEWISE) **still produced garbage**.

**WORKED (coherent), i.e. the differentiators:**
- **`DECODE_CUDAGRAPH_MODE=NONE` (eager decode)** — coherent, 3/3 prompts, MTP on and off.
- **Colocated single-node DP8/EP8** on the *same* v0.28 build/kernels/model (no remote KV) — coherent.
- **vLLM v0.27.1 + WideEP overlay** — the *same* PD-disagg path decodes coherently.

→ Coherent vs garbage turns on exactly **two conditions being simultaneously true: (1) the DSA sparse-MLA decode is captured in a CUDA graph, AND (2) it is consuming remotely-populated KV.** Removing *either* — run decode eager, or serve the same request colocated (locally-populated KV) — restores coherence. Reproduces on ≥2 DSA models (GLM-5.3-FP8, GLM-5.1-FP8). The corruption therefore lives in the **CUDA-grap

issues.title: [Bug][ROCm/gfx950] GLM-5.3-Flash 16K-chunk prefill: GPU memory-access fault when indexer triton kernels JIT during lazy CUDA-graph capture — clean under --enforce-eager
issues.body:
## GPU memory-access fault on gfx950 (MI350X) when triton kernels JIT during lazy CUDA-graph capture of a 16K-token chunked prefill (GLM-5.3-Flash, KDA/sparse-indexer path)

### Environment

- vLLM: `v0.28.1rc1.dev681+ge7edf17ce` (V1 engine), aiter @ `2693202`, triton 3.7.0
- Hardware: 8× AMD MI350X (gfx950), TP8 + expert-parallel
- Model: GLM-5.3-Flash fp8 (MLA + KDA sparse attention indexer → uses aiter `batched_gemm_a16wfp4`, `_gluon_fp8_mqa_logits`, `_cp_gather_indexer_quant_cache_gfx950_kernel`)
- Config: `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-model-len 524288 --enable-expert-parallel --distributed-executor-backend mp`, default `cudagraph_mode=FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, `VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1`

### Symptom

The **first** 16K-token chunk prefill crashes the engine with `Memory access fault` on all 8 ranks (e.g. `Memory access fault by GPU node-4 (Agent handle: 0x59ba0110) on address 0x7f733a000000. Reason: Unknown.`). Decode-only traffic and prefill chunks ≤8192 tokens are stable. Production impact: crash-looping pods on the first long-prompt request.

### Isolation: it's the graph capture, not the kernels

Differential with an identical request repro across cudagraph modes:

| Cudagraph mode | First 16K prefill |
|---|---|
| FULL | fault ×8 ranks |
| PIECEWISE | fault ×8 |
| FULL_AND_PIECEWISE | fault ×8 |
| **`--enforce-eager`** | **clean (0 faults, full repro suite)** |

At the moment of the fault, every kernel in the indexer chain is JIT-compiling *during inference* (boot warmup only exercised decode shapes; the 16K-prefill shapes are first seen at request time, when the 16384 cudagraph bucket is lazily captured):

```
WARNING [jit_monitor.py:141] Triton kernel JIT compilation during inference: BuildPrefillChunkMetadataKernel.kernel ...
WARNING [jit_monitor.py:141] Triton kernel JIT compilation during inference: _cp_gather_indexer_quant_cache_gfx950_kernel ...
WARNING [jit_monitor.py:141] Triton kernel JIT compilation during inference: _gluon_fp8_mqa_logits_kernel ...
WARNING [jit_monitor.py:141] Triton kernel JIT compilation during inference: _expand_pools_and_append_tail_kernel ...
WARNING [jit_monitor.py:141] Triton kernel JIT compilation during inference: _batched_gemm_a16wfp4_kernel ...
Memory access fault by GPU node-4 ...
```

### What we ruled out (in-server A/B, one full boot + repro per leg)

- Skipping `_gluon_fp8_mqa_logits` (correct-shape −inf logits substituted) → fault persists
- Skipping `_cp_gather_indexer_quant_cache_gfx950` (zero-fill) → fault persists
- Skipping `batched_gemm_a16wfp4` → **fault gone** (kernel execution required)
- Cloning **all** bmm tensor args (x, w, w_scales, y) to fresh contiguous memory in-server → fault persists (addresses innocent)
- `AMD_SERIALIZE_KERNEL=3` on/off → no effect
- Standalone replay with the **exact tensors dumped from the faulting call** (real strides/scales layout), M-sweep 4096→16000, workspace-pool carving with offset sweeps, two-stream interleave, plain `torch.cuda.CUDAGraph` capture, and fresh-variant-JIT-inside-plain-capture → **all clean**

So: the kernel is individually correct and capture-safe in isolation, eager execution is correct, but vLLM's lazy capture of the 16384 bucket (with fresh triton JIT in the same window) faults on gfx950. We could not reproduce it outside vLLM's capture machinery.

### Current workaround

`--enforce-eager` (fully stable at 16384) — at a significant decode-throughput cost. Chunk 8192 also avoids the fault but sacrifices prefill

issues.title: [Feature]: [CPU][GLM5Next][KDA] Add CPU KDA backend for GLM-5.3-Flash
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Motivation

GLM-5.3-Flash (`Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration`) is a hybrid model containing both:

* sparse MLA layers
* KDA (Kimi Delta Attention / gated delta-rule) linear-attention layers

Even if GLM5Next's sparse MLA / KeyPool path is made CPU-compatible, the model still cannot execute end-to-end on CPU without a KDA backend.

I would like to request native CPU support for GLM5Next KDA.

## Current state

The GLM5Next KDA implementation currently lives under the accelerator-specific path:

```text
vllm/models/glm5next/nvidia/kda.py
```

and uses GPU-oriented Flash Linear Attention / Triton operators such as:

```text
chunk_kda_with_fused_gate
fused_recurrent_kda
```

There does not appear to be a corresponding:

```text
vllm/models/glm5next/cpu/kda.py
```

or other CPU KDA execution path for GLM5Next on current `main`.

This makes KDA an independent CPU blocker from sparse MLA / KeyPool support.

GLM-5.3-Flash has a large number of KDA layers, so this cannot reasonably be worked around by supporting only the sparse-MLA portion of the model.

## Related CPU infrastructure already exists

The CPU backend already has substantial support for related linear-attention/state-space workloads.

In particular, current CPU platform code contains an accelerated GDN path using:

```text
AMX tiles
or
AVX-512 BF16 / VDPBF16PS
```

and vLLM already has CPU machinery for stateful hybrid models, including:

* recurrent state caches
* convolution state
* chunked prefill
* decode
* hybrid KV/state-cache management

KDA is not identical to GDN, but they are closely related enough that it may be possible to reuse much of this infrastructure.

## KDA-specific work

As I understand it, GLM5Next KDA needs CPU equivalents for the KDA-specific operations around the existing gated-delta/state machinery, including:

```text
Q/K/V short convolution
        │
        ▼
KDA gate computation
        │
        ▼
chunked gated-delta prefill
        │
        ▼
final recurrent state
        │
        ▼
single-token recurrent decode
        │
        ▼
gated/RMSNorm output
```

The important parts include:

* q/k/v convolution and convolution-state update
* KDA gate calculation
* per-channel decay/gating behavior
* `chunk_kda_with_fused_gate` equivalent for prefill
* `fused_recurrent_kda` equivalent for decode
* initial-state gathering
* final-state writeback
* mixed decode/prefill handling
* state-cache addressing
* chunk boundaries
* prefix-cache/state restore correctness

## Requested feature

Add a CPU KDA backend for GLM5Next.

A correctness-first implementation would be useful even before full AMX optimization.

One possible structure could be:

```text
vllm/models/glm5next/
├── common/
├── nvidia/
├── amd/
└── cpu/
    └── kda.py
```

with explicit platform dispatch rather than allowing CPU to reach the NVIDIA implementation.

## Possible implementation phases

### Phase 1: reference CPU implementation

Provide a functional PyTorch/C++ CPU implementation for:

* short convolution
* chunked KDA prefill
* recurrent KDA decode
* KDA gate/output
* state gather/scatter

The initial goal would be correctness and end-to-end execution.

### Phase 2: reuse existing CPU GDN kernels

Where the mathematical operations overlap with the existing CPU GDN backend, share or extend those implementations rather than creating duplicate infrastructure.

### Phase 3: x86 optimization

Optimize the expensive GEMM/state operations with:

* A

issues.title: [Feature]: Plan for enabling mypy in tests directory
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**Goal:** Enable MyPy static checking in the `/tests` directory.

**Implementation:** Move `tests/**` from `--follow-imports skip` to `--follow-imports silent` in [`tools/pre_commit/mypy.py`](../../tools/pre_commit/mypy.py), one directory at a time, **with each PR enforcing the directories it fixed**.

Partial: #26533

/cc @hmellor @yewentao256

---

### Plan

**Note:** Errors below were measured with
`mypy --python-version 3.10 --follow-imports silent <dir>` — the target state for each directory.

---

#### Blocker: removing a directory from `SEPARATE_GROUPS` enforces nothing

`group_files()` iterates `SEPARATE_GROUPS` in **list order** and `break`s on the
first prefix match. `"tests"` is the first entry, so every `tests/**` file is
claimed by it:

```python
>>> group_files(['tests/config/test_multimodal_config.py',
...              'tests/v1/shutdown/test_processor_error.py'])
{'tests': [both files]}     # never lands in 'tests/config' or 'tests/v1/shutdown'
```

A file only gets `follow_imports=silent` by matching **no** entry at all and
falling through to the `""` group. Since `"tests"` matches everything under
`tests/`, no per-directory removal can ever take effect before `"tests"` itself
is removed — which is the very last step.

**Sorting `SEPARATE_GROUPS` by longest prefix does not fix this** (verified):
with `tests/config` removed, its files still match `tests` and still run with
`skip`. Sorting only changes which *skip* group a file lands in, which is
cosmetic today.

Consequence if the plan is executed as originally written: every PR from 1
through kv-C fixes real errors but enforces none of them, and all of that work is
free to regress until the final PR. **PR 0 below fixes the mechanism so that
stops being true.**

---

#### PR 0 — Make per-directory enforcement possible (prerequisite) (#49570) **DONE**

Add an allowlist of verified-clean directories, matched **before**
`SEPARATE_GROUPS`, that routes files into the `""` group (no `--follow-imports`
flag → pyproject's `silent`):

```python
# Directories verified clean under follow_imports=silent. Checked before
# SEPARATE_GROUPS; these files join the "" group and are enforced at silent.
# Moving a directory from SEPARATE_GROUPS to here is what makes a fix stick.
SILENT_GROUPS: list[str] = []
```

In `group_files()`, before the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop:

```python
if any(re.match(f"^{d}.*", changed_file) for d in SILENT_GROUPS):
    file_groups[""].append(changed_file)
    continue
```

Also sort the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop by descending path length so sub-directory
groups stop being shadowed by their parents. This is cosmetic today (all those
groups run at `skip`) but keeps the per-group log labels honest as directories
drain.

Verified behaviour with `SILENT_GROUPS = ["tests/config", "tests/v1/shutdown"]`:

```python
{'':                    ['tests/config/a.py', 'tests/v1/shutdown/b.py', 'vllm/x.py'],
 'tests/compile/passes': ['tests/compile/passes/d.py'],
 'tests/v1/core':        ['tests/v1/core/c.py']}
```

Clean dirs are enforced at `silent`; everything unfixed keeps its `skip` group;
`"tests"` can stay in `SEPARATE_GROUPS` until the very end.

**Bundle PR 0 into PR 1** rather than shipping it alone — AGENTS.md discourages
standalone mechanical PRs, and PR 1 gives it substantive work to ride along with.

issues.title: [RFC]: Share KV transfer planning primitives across KV connectors
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

#### Problem

Cross-engine KV transfer (PD disaggregation) must, per cache group, classify the KV cache spec type (attention / SSM / other) and compute how local TP shards map onto a remote engine's TP shards — slice by TP ratio, replicate, or copy whole. When this is wrong it usually fails silently: mismatched slicing corrupts state (e.g. conv-state bytes landing in the wrong sub-projection).

The only in-tree implementation of this planning logic lives inside the NIXL connector (`nixl/tp_mapping.py`, underscore-private helpers). The cost is observable today:

- The same subtle bugs get fixed twice. Mamba prefill truncation ordering was fixed independently in #53523 (NIXL) and #53663 (Mooncake) within the same week.
- New model architectures need connector-specific fixes on the Mooncake side (#52516, #53078, #55523), while NIXL absorbs the same class of change through generic machinery (#53780).
- Reuse is already happening piecemeal: #53078 reuses `derive_mamba_conv_split` from `v1/ssm_conv_transfer_utils.py`, a framework extraction from NIXL.

#### Proposal

Make this planning logic a shared connector-framework module with a public, connector-agnostic API, and migrate connectors onto it in stages:

1. **Substrate** (draft: #57309). `v1/transfer_planning.py` hosts spec-type classification (`is_attention_spec`, `is_ssm_spec`, `get_representative_spec_type`) and local-to-remote TP mapping (`TPMapping`, `compute_tp_mapping`). NIXL consumes it unchanged; MooncakeConnector adopts the classification helpers; contract tests pin the classification vocabulary. NIXL-specific structs (e.g. `ReadSpec`) stay NIXL-local.
2. **Region descriptions.** Extract the per-region transfer-description construction from `nixl/base_worker.py` registration into the same module, so a connector declares region facts (type, layout, shard rule) and the shared code computes the plan. NIXL behavior unchanged.
3. **MooncakeConnector adoption.** Replace the private region planning (`_get_transfer_regions` and related) with the shared planner after #53078 / #55523 land and provide the behavioral baseline. Wire format unchanged.

Invariants across all stages: NIXL behavior unchanged, wire formats unchanged, and connector-specific concerns (transports, the Mooncake Store canonical layout) stay connector-local.

### Alternatives

- **Status quo (two implementations)**: correctness fixes must be applied twice (#53523 / #53663) and the copies drift over time.
- **Mooncake imports from the `nixl` package**: a layering violation — it couples one connector to another connector's private internals, so every NIXL change risks breaking it.
- **Single big-bang migration**: harder to review and bisect; the substrate stage is independently useful to any connector.

### Additional context

- Stage 1 is open as draft PR #57309, including the duplicate-work check against open PRs.
- I am willing to implement and maintain the follow-up stages. Feedback from NIXL and Mooncake connector maintainers on the stage-2/3 boundary would be appreciated.

### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment (TDX guest with an H100 in Confidential Computing mode)</summary>

```text
OS                           : Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS (x86_64), kernel 7.0.0-31-generic (Intel TDX guest, 16 vCPU / 64 GB)
Python version               : 3.12.14
PyTorch version              : 2.13.0+cu130
CUDA used to build PyTorch   : 13.0
Nvidia driver version        : 595.91.07 (Canonical-signed open kernel modules)
GPU 0                        : NVIDIA H100 NVL (PCIe passthrough via vfio-pci / iommufd)
vLLM Version                 : 0.29.0 (PyPI wheel)
flashinfer                   : 0.6.18

$ nvidia-smi conf-compute -q
CC State                   : ON
Multi-GPU Mode             : None
CPU CC Capabilities        : INTEL TDX
$ nvidia-smi conf-compute -grs
Confidential Compute GPUs Ready state: ready

Host: Ubuntu 26.04.1, kernel 7.0.0-31 (kvm_intel.tdx=1), QEMU 10.2.1, GPU switched to CC mode with
gpu-admin-tools (--set-cc-mode=on). The same guest runs transformers / CuPy / plain torch correctly.
```
</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On a GPU in NVIDIA Confidential Computing (CC) mode inside a TDX guest, vLLM 0.29.0 with the default (V2) GPU model runner **starts fine and serves requests, but every response is garbage**, for example `!!!!!!!!` (token id 0 repeated) or `[][][][]`. There is no error or warning anywhere, and the same model produces correct output with plain `transformers` on the same GPU, so this is easy to misattribute to the GPU or the CC setup. Setting `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` makes the output correct.

**Root cause (verified):** the V2 model runner feeds `input_ids`, positions, block tables etc. to the GPU through UVA views of pinned host memory (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/buffer_utils.py` → `UvaBuffer` → `get_accelerator_view_from_cpu_tensor` → `torch.ops._C.get_cuda_view_from_cpu_tensor`). Under GPU CC the device cannot access guest memory directly (all host/device traffic goes through the driver's encrypted bounce buffers), and the UVA view **does not follow later host writes**: the GPU keeps reading the contents the buffer had when it was mapped. The model therefore sees all-zero `input_ids` and confidently predicts token 0 at every position. Prompt logprobs make this visible: with `prompt_logprobs=1` every prompt position predicts `!` with logprob ≈ 0.

Minimal reproduction of the UVA behaviour (no model needed), run inside the CC guest:

```python
import torch, vllm  # importing vllm loads the _C ops
cpu = torch.arange(1, 9, dtype=torch.int32).pin_memory()
gpu_view = torch.ops._C.get_cuda_view_from_cpu_tensor(cpu)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("initial          cpu:", cpu.tolist(), " gpu view:", (gpu_view + 0).tolist())
cpu.fill_(99); torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("after host write cpu:", cpu.tolist(), " gpu view:", (gpu_view + 0).tolist())
dst = torch.empty_like(cpu, device="cuda"); dst.copy_(cpu, non_blocking=True); torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("explicit H2D copy       :", dst.tolist())
```

Output on the CC GPU:

```text
initial          cpu: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]  gpu view: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
after host write cpu: [99, 99, 99, 99, 99, 99, 99, 99]  gpu view: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]   <-- stale
explicit H2D copy       : [99, 99, 99, 99, 99, 99, 99, 99]
```

Ordinary pinned and pageable H2D/D2H copies (blocking and `non_blocking=True`) are all correct on the same GPU; only the zero-copy UVA view is stale.

issues.title: [Bug]: bench serve drops custom headers when stopping the profiler
issues.body:
### Your current environment

Benchmark source from main `cd64c2d`, run in the official vLLM 0.28.0 Linux arm64 CPU image (`sha256:dbc1b4da66bbc0cb3a3f6859cd9046833f9540d34322b192625868f888e8e094`). SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, float32, eager mode, PyTorch CPU profiler. The server runs behind a local forwarding proxy that requires the supplied headers for POST requests.

### Describe the bug

`vllm bench serve --profile --header ...` passes custom headers to `/start_profile` and inference requests, but leaves them out of `/stop_profile`. With a proxy requiring those headers, inference completes but the stop request gets HTTP 401. The profiler stays active and has not exported its trace when the benchmark finishes.

For a header-protected server configured with `--profiler-config '{"profiler":"torch","torch_profiler_dir":"/traces"}'`, run:

```sh
vllm bench serve \
  --base-url http://localhost:8080 \
  --model smollm2-e2e --tokenizer HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 8 --random-output-len 3 \
  --num-prompts 2 --max-concurrency 1 --profile \
  --header 'Authorization=Bearer local-validation' 'X-Tenant=contributions-e2e'
```

The header values above are disposable validation values. This also reproduces with `--backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions`.

Observed for both backends:

```text
POST /start_profile      200  both custom headers present
POST /v1/...completions  200  both custom headers present
POST /stop_profile       401  custom headers absent
completed requests: 2; failed inference requests: 0
CPU trace files at benchmark completion: 0
```

The stop request should retain the same custom headers as the start request. Adding `extra_headers=extra_headers` to its `RequestFuncInput` fixes both backends. Afterward `/stop_profile` returns 200 and a gzip trace containing CPU operations is exported. Unprotected controls and generated text/token counts are unchanged.

Searched existing issues and PRs for profiler/header/authentication combinations. #55536 changes server-side endpoint authentication; this report is about the benchmark client dropping user-supplied headers and reproduces through an authenticating proxy without that PR.

Prepared and tested with Codex.

issues.title: [RFC]: Asymmetric P/D Deployment for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash
issues.body:
## Summary. DeepSeek-V4.1's bounded-replay structure creates an opportunity to make Prefill/Decode disaggregation substantially more asymmetric. Today, a Prefill worker still loads the full 40-layer model even though, after layer 20, only the final 128 prompt tokens need to be processed. This keeps almost half of the model weights resident on P for a small decoder-layer workload whose MoE utilization is likely poor. This RFC proposes moving that final 128-token window entirely to the Decode worker: - For a prompt of length `N`, P computes only `[0, N-128)` and transfers the resulting prefix KV state. - D computes `[N-128, N)` as its first full-model step and samples the first output token. - The request then continues through normal speculative decode with `q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens`. This asymmetry has two main benefits. - First, P would load only the causal encoder plus the minimal layer-20 KV/Indexer projection path, potentially removing close to half of its transformer-layer weights; a key target is fitting a production Prefill replica on one B300 GPU. - Second, moving the decoder-layer work to D increases the computational intensity of that work by executing it as part of D's much larger token batches, improving utilization relative to processing the 128-token replay on P. The execution model on D also becomes simpler than layer-local decoder replay. D never needs separate encoder and decoder token batches: ```text first D step: all L0-L39 process the same 128 prompt tokens later D steps: all L0-L39 process the same 1 + num_spec_tokens tokens ``` The trade-off is that each newly admitted request contributes 128 bounded-prefill tokens to a D step, which can temporarily increase the Decode token count and affect ITL (TPOT). This incremental cost is expected to be modest for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash: its light KV cache permits large Decode batches, and DSpark also makes each Decode batch process many tokens. Against that baseline, adding 128 tokens when a new request is admitted is a relatively small increase. This RFC is a design proposal for discussion. I do not currently plan to implement it, and there is no prototype or benchmark result yet. Implementation ownership is open. ## Proposed Change. ### Model placement and token ownership ```mermaid flowchart LR I[Prompt: N tokens] I -->|Prefix: N-W tokens| P I -->|Final window: W tokens| D subgraph P[Prefill worker: partial model] PE[Causal encoder L0-L19] PK[Minimal L20 Main-KV / Indexer
projection path] PE --> PK end subgraph D[Decode worker: full model] BR[First step: bounded prefill
L0-L39, q_len = W] FT[Sample first output token] ND[Later steps: speculative decode
L0-L39, q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens] BR --> FT --> ND end P -->|Prefix Main / Indexer KV| D ``` For prompts no longer than `W`, P performs no model forward and D processes the complete prompt. Conceptually, P would retain: - embeddings and complete layers L0-L19; - the minimal layer-20 projections needed to produce its canonical C1 Main KV and Indexer K; and - the state required by the KV connector handoff. P would not retain the complete layer-20 attention/MoE path, layers 21–39, final normalization, or the LM head. ### Request flow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant P as Prefill worker participant D as Decode worker P->>P: Run prompt prefix [0, N-W) P->>P: Produce prefix Main

issues.title: [RFC]: Support ViT Full CUDA Graph (Tracker)
issues.body:
### Motivation.

Multimodal large language models (e.g., Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5, GLM-V, Kimi K2.5) rely on a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder to process visual inputs before feeding them into the language model backbone. In production serving scenarios, the ViT forward pass involves launching a large number of small CUDA kernels — including patch embedding, layer normalization, multi-head self-attention, and MLP projections — each of which incurs non-trivial kernel launch overhead on the host side.

Currently, vLLM supports CUDA graph capture for the decoder (LLM) portion of the model, which has proven effective at reducing kernel launch costs and improving throughput. However, the ViT encoder is still executed eagerly, meaning every forward pass re-launches all kernels from scratch. Extending full CUDA graph support to the ViT encoder would allow the entire encoder forward pass to be captured and replayed as a single graph, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead and enabling more consistent, low-latency inference for multimodal models.

issues.title: [RFC]: Limit the use of envvars in vLLM
issues.body:
### Motivation.

vLLM's envvars are on the edge of getting out of control. There are many envvars should instead be configs. Like the attention backend, all2all kernel backend, and even there is a flag to control KV cache layout. envvars are evil because:

1. It is equivalent of using global variables everywhere in the code, which is a bad programming practice.
2. envvars have no advanced structure like, hierarchy, typechecks, etc. 

In summary, I think envvars are the kind of thing that is very easy to add so people tend to add envvars as the shortest path to implement their feature, but this can quickly becomes unmanageable and makes the project very hard to use. 

### Proposed Change.

I think we should:

1. Spend some effort on reviewing the current envvars and move many of them to configs.
2. Have very strict bar on what can be an envvar and question every new envvars in vllm.

### Feedback Period.

issues.title: [Feature]: Optimize collectives in TP MoE case using torch.compile pass
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

To avoid redundant work in MoE models in the TP case, sequence parallelism was added to the Deepseek model definition in #24134 and expanded to other models in #24982. However, to avoid performing surgery on the linear layer, the current approach performs more communication than necessary. With a torch.compile custom pass, we can rewrite the graph to remove the redundant computation.

### More details

Before the SP optimization, the ops in the model were:
```
- o_proj:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...] (incomplete results)
- all_reduce:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- rms_norm:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- router:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- experts:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- ...
```

With sequence parallel enabled, this becomes:
```
- o_proj: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...] (incomplete results)
- all_reduce: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- rms_norm:[num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
- chunk: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- router: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- experts: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- all_gather: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
```

Additionally, experts now properly do the dp+tp<->ep dispatch instead of just the original replicated dp<->ep dispatch.

Notice that the `all_reduce` (and `rms_norm`) do redundant communication as each TP rank only requires partial results. With a compile pass, we can convert the `all_reduce` -> `rms_norm` -> `chunk` sequence into a `reduce_scatter` -> `rms_norm`:

```
- o_proj: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...] (incomplete results)
- reduce_scatter: [num_tokens, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- router: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- experts: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens/tp, ...]
- all_gather: [num_tokens/tp, ...] -> [num_tokens, ...]
```

We should create a new `SequenceParallelismMoEPass`, controlled by a new `PassConfig.enable_sp_moe` flag (following the new naming convention in #27995) so that it can be turned on independently of regular SP. We will likely need to pad the number of tokens to a multiple of TP size, although like described in #29136, there are alternatives.

#### SP
Additionally, to make SP-MoE compatible with AsyncTP, the SP pass should also replace the `all_gather` -> `rms_norm` sequence with `rms_norm` -> `all_gather`, such that the `all_gather` can be fused with the following QKV proj. We can see that in the SP case we perform an `all_gather` instead of `all_reduce` after the MLP layer.

### Alternatives

Alternatively, the original optimization could be done as a compile pass as well, which would significantly clean up the MoE model definitions. However, that would mean that `VLLM_COMPILE` compilation mode would be required for this optimization and if compilation is disabled, the optimization would be disabled as well. Generally we accept lower performance in eager mode as compilation is on by default, but I know there was a reason this was done this way (don't remember why).

We could also just let the SP pass first transform `all_reduce` -> `rms_norm` into `reduce_scatter` -> `rms_norm` -> `all_gather` and then eliminate the `all_gather` -> `chunk` combo. But then we have less control over SP after MoE (although it seems like all_reduce is not even used in that case).

### Additional context

Original proposal comment: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/24982#pullrequest

issues.title: Upgrade to Transformers v5
issues.body:
## What is this issue?

This issue serves as a living tracker for the current issues preventing us from upgrading vLLM to Transformers v5.

We will use sub-issues to track individual failures and PRs should be made against these sub-issues.

The solutions to these issues may need to be applied to either:

- Transformers in the form of:
  - Adding missing backward compatibility (usually for custom code models)
  - General bug fixes/improvements to new features of v5
- vLLM in the form of:
  - Forward compatibility with how something is now done in v5
  - Edge case handling for issues that v4 ignored (such as config validation)

Sometimes, the issue is simply with the model checkpoint itself, for example if it:

- Contains a malformed `config.json` that cannot be used to instantiate the newly input validated `PreTrainedConfig` class
- Custom code* uses deprecated/removed APIs

In these situations, the best solution will likely be to skip these tests in vLLM and open a PR to Transformers to contribute this model. This will be faster and more sustainable than waiting for the model vendor to fix their custom model code, sometimes they nevert do.

Contributing the new model should be done using the new [Modular Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/modular_transformers) so that the implementation is easy to maintain and will remain maintained by the Transformers team.

_*particularly in the parts of the model implementation that vLLM tries to directly reuse, such as config/tokenizer/multimodal processor_

## Comprehensive list of skips

Now that the parent PR is merged we have a comprehensive list of all tests that are currently skipped on `main`

issues.title: [Feature]: `CustomOp` cleanup
issues.body:
### 🚀 Motivation

Currently, we do not have a consistent plan for "light" custom ops (subclasses of `CustomOp` with both torch-native and GPU implementations). As we work on improved performance on NVIDIA Blackwell and AMD, we should be more intentional with CompilationConfig defaults that control custom op dispatching. This is a parent issue that tracks smaller PRs addressing `CustomOp`s.

In vLLM, there are two kinds of custom kernels/ops:
1. "heavy" ops like GEMMs, MoE, and attention, which will mostly use tuned custom kernels for maximum performance.
2. "light" ops like `RMSNorm`, `SiluAndMul`, and `RoPE`, which have both torch-native and custom GPU implementations.

This issue only refers to "light" ops, which are (or should be) all subclasses of `CustomOp`.

When we enabled `torch.compile` by default in V1, the plan was to reduce our reliance on custom kernels to reduce maintenance costs and code complexity, even with minor performance costs. Recent versions of `torch` actually produce Triton kernels faster than our custom op implementations anyway.

However, with startup time concerns (#19824), it seems like we want good performance even with Inductor disabled (more discussion on startup times to come in a follow-up issue). Additionally, custom op performance has been reported to be better than torch.compile-generated Triton kernels on AMD.

### ❗ Issues

This is a list of current issues with custom ops. The following section tracks proposed and WIP solutions. Larger line items might have their own issue or get one in the future.

1. [Perf] FP8 quantization not fused with rms_norm/silu_mul (because fp8 quant doesn't have a torch native implementation)
2. [Perf] AMD uses custom ops but fusion for them is hardcoded to disabled.
3. [Perf] We don't have good visibility into performance differences between GPU and torch native implementations of custom ops across different models and hardware platforms.
4. [Perf][Code Quality] Fused and unfused custom ops currently reimplement the same code, and only some are vectorized.
5. [Testing] Custom op tests either don't exist or reimplement Torch naive implementations
6. [Compilation] Current custom passes rely on custom op pattern matching, which involves auto-functionalization (#14703) and requires custom ops to be enabled. If custom ops are slower than native impls, that means e.g. attention+quant fusion needs to take a hit on other quants to fuse the o-proj one. I'll create an RFC for this.

### ✅  Solutions

Once we have benchmarking numbers, we can set sensible defaults. Improving startup time will likely result in more explicit "profiles" with better config defaults.

Detailed solution tracking:

1. ✅ @ProExpertProg: FP8 `CustomOp`s in #19830
2. ✅ #19181 removed hardcoded `enable_fusion=False`.
3. 🚧 WIP @gshtras and @SageMoore are collecting some benchmarking numbers for custom op performance. More benchmarking can be done as needed. Automating some of this would be great as well.
4. ❗ TODO consolidating, vectorizing and cleaning up CUDA/HIP implementations of custom ops.
5. ❗ TODO add testing utilities for custom ops.
6. ✅ match and perform fusion with custom ops disabled: #24604

#### ➕ Other potential improvements

- [ ] Simplify custom op enablement
- [ ] Improve custom op documentation
- [ ] Custom op microbenchmarks

issues.title: [Docs] Document NIXL KV connector metrics aggregation semantics
issues.body:
## Summary

The NIXL KV connector logs transfer metrics periodically:

```
KV Transfer metrics: Num successful transfers=4, Avg xfer time (ms)=1.381, P90 xfer time (ms)=2.601, Avg post time (ms)=0.672, P90 post time (ms)=0.801, Avg MB per transfer=2.25, Throughput (MB/s)=1629.549, Avg number of descriptors=72.0
```

Currently there is no documentation explaining what these metrics represent, especially in the context of **multi-rank (TP > 1) deployments**. This has already caused confusion among users.

## Current behavior

All metrics are **aggregated across all TP ranks** before summary stats are computed:

1. Each TP rank independently records per-transfer telemetry (`transfer_duration`, `post_duration`, `bytes_transferred`, `num_descriptors`) via `NixlKVConnectorStats.record_transfer()` in [`stats.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py).
2. Stats from all ranks are concatenated via `aggregate()` (`list.extend()`).
3. `reduce()` computes averages, percentiles, and throughput over the **combined** pool of observations from all ranks.

This means:
- **"Num successful transfers"** is the total count across all ranks, not per-rank.
- **"Avg MB per transfer"** is the average over all individual rank-level transfers, not the total bytes moved for a single KV cache transfer operation.
- **"Throughput (MB/s)"** is `total_MB_all_ranks / total_time_all_ranks` — effectively an average per-rank throughput, not the aggregate system throughput.
- **Percentiles (P90)** are computed over the combined distribution of all ranks' transfer times.

This is unintuitive because users may expect metrics to reflect per-engine totals or aggregate system throughput.

## What needs to be documented

1. **Docstrings in `stats.py`**: Add clear documentation to `NixlKVConnectorStats` explaining that stats are aggregated across all TP ranks and what each metric represents in that context.
2. **Inline comments in `reduce()`**: Clarify the semantics of throughput and averages — that they are per-rank averages over the combined observation pool.
3. **Docstrings in `metrics.py`**: Document the `observe()` → `aggregate()` → `reduce()` → `log()` pipeline and the fact that stats arrive pre-aggregated across workers.
4. **(Optional) Docs page**: Add a section to the disaggregated serving documentation explaining how to interpret the KV Transfer metrics log line.

## Relevant files

- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py` — `NixlKVConnectorStats` (recording, aggregation, reduction)
- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/metrics.py` — `KVConnectorLogging` (observe/log pipeline), `KVConnectorStats` (base class)

## Context

See related discussion: metrics are aggregated across ranks rather than reported per-rank or per-engine. This is a deliberate design choice (fire-and-forget from workers), but it needs to be clearly documented so users can correctly interpret the numbers.

issues.title: [Transformers v5] InternVL2
issues.body:
This is a sub-issue forming part of the work in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38379, please read the description of this issue before beginning to work on this one.

## Which test is failing?

Transformers v5 creates the model on the meta device first, then loads the weights, similarly to what vLLM does. The issue here is that the custom model code in the checkpoint tries to use real tensors as part of model structure construction.

Since the issue here is with the HF reference generation, this cannot be fixed in vLLM (other than skipping the tests until the model works with Transformers v5). The proper solution to this issue is to upstream this architecture, which shouldn't be too hard using Modular Transformers as the text backbone is Qwen2 so that can be reused.

```console
$ pytest tests/models/multimodal/generation/test_common.py::test_single_image_models[intern_vl-test_case25]
...
RuntimeError: Tensor.item() cannot be called on meta tensors
```

## How to configure my environment?

It's very important that you install both vLLM and Transformers from source so that your test results reflect the current state of both libraries.

```console
# Or your fork
git clone https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git
git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git

cd vllm
VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install -e .
uv pip install -e ../transformers
```

issues.title: [Bug]: ModelOpt Llama-4 Checkpoints Take 5+ minutes to load
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

In working on some MoE refactors, I discovered that L4 for ModelOpt takes 5+minutes to load weights even from CPU page cache. 
- https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8

The root cause is basically this hack logic to load the state dict that ModelOpt uses
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/models/llama4.py#L439-L523 [modelopt is the fused case] 

What happens is that the CPU tensor (loaded weight) that we are going to load into the GPU tensor (param) becomes non-contiguous due to this logic. As a result, when we eventually call `_copy()` from CPU->GPU we are calling this on a non-contiguous cpu tensor which takes 3-4s per weight.

To hack around this for local R&D, I simply immediately move the loaded_weight to the GPU. This makes the gather happen on the GPU which accelerates things a lot. This isn't reasonable as an actual solution though

We should investigate where the logic in the weight loader can avoid creating non-contiguous CPU tensors

issues.title: [torch.compile] E2E correctness testing for fusions
issues.body:
E2E tests for fusions (`tests/compile/fusions_e2e`) have done a great job preventing fusion regressions where model/forward code changes break a custom torch.compile fusion pass. However, we currently have no way of testing correctness for these fusion configurations.

It would be good to investigate an approach where we only run a few layers of a model and compare the outputs. This would be helpful for correctness testing in general, and we could compare the outputs to both a baseline vLLM configuration and the huggingface baseline.

This would likely require some work to fix weight loading for models like DeepSeek when `--hf-overrides.num_hidden_layers` is overriden.

issues.title: [Feature]: Priority scheduling supports preemption of requests in the running queue by requests in the waiting queue
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

The current priority scheduling only supports evicting low-priority requests from the running queue when resources are insufficient. However, when scheduling the waiting queue, if pending requests cannot be scheduled (for example, when the number of requests in the running queue has reached max_num_seqs), even high-priority requests cannot preempt requests in the running queue.

issues.body:

Sometimes Flashinfer will compile for 10mins without a single log, making it easy to think it's a hang. Would be good to add a progress bar or at least a simple log.

See https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38241 for more info. Note that this was without `flashinfer-jit-cache` installed.
